episode_summary: August 2019 episode 269 with hosts Corey and D, the first show after Cello left the podcast. They explain proof of work versus proof of stake: what each one stakes, Sybil or civil resistance, the longest-chain rule and double spending, the history from CPUs to GPUs to ASICs, energy use and coal, and why they want to think in satoshis.

cards.claim: In August 2019 the hosts announced that Cello had stepped away from the show after long-running disagreements, leaving Corey and D as the hosts.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: Cello has decided to step away and leave.

cards.claim: In August 2019 the hosts said Bitcoin and Ethereum were both proof-of-work systems, secured by computers solving a very large Sudoku-like puzzle.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: they're both secured by computers playing the equivalent of what would be a very large Sudoku puzzle

cards.claim: In August 2019 the hosts said Ethereum was transitioning toward Ethereum 2.0, a proof-of-stake system.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: So Ethereum is working on moving, transitioning towards F2.0, which is a proof of stake system.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said proof of work means putting an external resource up front, usually your energy bill and mining hardware.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: proof of work typically means you're putting an external resource up front. And that's usually in the form of your energy bill

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said proof of stake means putting all of your money into an internal resource, the coin of the network itself.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: And proof of stake, you're putting all of your money into an internal resource of the system, namely the coin of that network.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host explained that civil, or Sybil, resistance means you cannot spin up many fake identities to sway a vote.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: What that means is that you can't just spin up a bunch of fake people and pretend to vote to try and sway a vote

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said stake-based voting works because a participant must put up a resource they do not want to lose for each vote.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: They have to have stake in the game. They need to put a resource up front that they don't want to lose.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said the original point of Bitcoin was solving the double spending problem.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: The original bullet point of Bitcoin was it solved the double spending problem.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host described Nakamoto consensus as the golden rule that nodes add blocks only to the longest chain.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: I'm only going to add to the longest one. That's the golden rule.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host explained that cheating the longest-chain rule requires mining several blocks in a row and submitting them together, which needs more work than available resources allow.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: mine multiple blocks in a row so that you can make the adjustment you want and submit them all at the same time, which is more work than is capable of being done based on the available resources

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said the energy pumped into Bitcoin was larger than the output of many countries, though it was still smaller than some.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: pumped into Bitcoin is, you know, larger than a lot of countries output.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said you cannot solve the energy problem with an off switch, and proof of work was not going anywhere soon.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: you can't always just solve a problem with an off switch. You've got to kind of build your way there

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host described the original Bitcoin idea of one CPU, one vote, with commodity hardware and no mining pools.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: The idea was one CPU, one vote. It was commoditized hardware.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host defined mining efficiency as the number of SHA-256 hashes per second obtained for a given amount of energy.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: By efficiently, I mean turn the same or less amount of wattage or kilowatt hours

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said mining moved from CPUs to GPUs and then to ASICs, which are application specific integrated circuits.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: we can actually make specific pieces of hardware we call them asics now application specific integrated circuit

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said ASICs made commodity hardware worthless for contributing to Bitcoin mining.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: It basically makes all of the computation that we have as like normal commoditized hardware that everyone has access to is worthless

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said Bitcoin's energy mix right then mostly came from coal.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: Right now, it mostly comes from coal. That's a problem.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said proof of stake can punish misbehavior by slashing stake, while proof of work only offers incentives.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: So there's incentives and disincentives to behave correctly with a proof-of-stake system. You cannot do that with a proof-of-work system.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said proof-of-work miners can move hash power to another chain such as BCash, which proof-of-stake stake cannot do.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: if I'm trying to mine there I can take it and mine on Bcash

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said he leaned toward proof of stake because it might give the same security as proof of work without needlessly running SHA-256.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: I lean towards proof-of-stake systems because I think there's a potential that they'll be able to provide

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said that Bitcoin being worth global GDP was not going to happen anytime soon, or probably ever.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: That's not going to happen anytime soon or probably ever for that matter.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host calculated that if all bitcoin were worth global GDP, one satoshi would be about a cent.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: then one Satoshi would be around half a cent to a cent, one penny.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host predicted that thinking in satoshis would happen quickly, but more slowly in Western nations than in other countries.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: It can happen really quick. It just won't happen in the Western nations as quickly as it would happen in the other countries.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said Bitcoin forces everyone to adopt the mental model that people in other nations already use for large numbers.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: it's almost like Bitcoin forces everyone to go to what other nations have been doing naturally for a very long time.

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host urged the community to start thinking and pricing in satoshis, to make bitcoin more accessible.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: hey guys we're thinking in satoshis now and i know we tried it before but this might be a good time

cards.claim: In August 2019 a host said the Winklevoss twins held tens of thousands of bitcoin, which would be trillions of satoshis.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: Tens of thousands, right? They would have instead have trillions of Satoshis, right?

title: The Bitcoin Podcast #269: Proof of Work vs. Proof of Stake
